papers.research_question: How can we interpret the hidden embeddings of large language models in natural language to reveal their internal reasoning and enable control over model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SelfIE, a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own hidden embeddings in natural language, and extends it to control model behavior via supervised and reinforcement control on embeddings.
papers.conclusion: SelfIE provides a powerful framework for interpreting and controlling LLM reasoning by generating text descriptions of hidden embeddings, opening avenues for transparent and reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SelfIE can elicit implicit world state knowledge in embeddings without training, matching the performance of a 100-shot linear probe.
SelfIE reveals internal reasoning processes behind complex LLM behaviors such as harmful knowledge recall, prompt injection, ethical decisions, physics reasoning, social reasoning, and hallucination.
SelfIE-based supervised control can edit fact associations and open-ended concepts with good generalization, requiring gradient computation only for individual layers.
SelfIE-based reinforcement control can erase harmful knowledge in LLMs without supervised targets, reducing prompt injection success rate by 84.66%.
SelfIE-based control can override user-specified ethical preferences, increasing fairness in LLM responses with a 95% effective rate.
future_direction: Further exploration of reasoning patterns in LLMs and model reasoning behavior controls with hidden embeddings.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM's reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE's text descriptions on hidden embeddings also open up new avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how LLMs develop causally functional representations of semantic roles, specifically focusing on the localization, emergence dynamics, and cross-scale/cross-family generalization of semantic-role circuits.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a causal-temporal method for discovering and tracking semantic-role circuits in LLMs, and finds that these circuits are highly localized, emerge via gradual refinement, and show partial transfer across scales and architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure that exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures, suggesting that transformers encode predicate-argument binding via compact circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic-role information is encoded in compact, role-specific circuits (89–92% attribution within ≤20 nodes).
These circuits emerge via continuous refinement rather than discrete phase transitions.
There is a structure-function dissociation: circuits stabilize structurally before becoming functionally indispensable.
Cross-scale and cross-family analysis shows moderate component reuse (24–51% node overlap) but divergent wiring.
Larger models reuse similar components while rewiring connections.
papers.abstract: Despite displaying semantic competence, large language models' internal mechanisms that ground abstract semantic structure remain insufficiently characterised. We propose a method integrating role-cross minimal pairs, temporal emergence analysis, and cross-model comparison to study how LLMs implement semantic roles. Our analysis uncovers: (i) highly concentrated circuits (89-94% attribution within 28 nodes); (ii) gradual structural refinement rather than phase transitions, with larger models sometimes bypassing localised circuits; and (iii) moderate cross-scale conservation (24-59% component overlap) alongside high spectral similarity. These findings suggest that LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure, and these mechanisms exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Revisiting Modality Invariance in a Multilingual Speech-Text Model via Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How and when do multilingual speech–text models reuse shared circuitry across modalities, and how does this reuse differ between input-language representation and output-language generation during decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-step-aware framework for cross-modal evaluation of multilingual speech-text models, revealing that cross-modal language alignment is time- and function-dependent, with representation alignment strongest at early steps and control alignment strengthening later.
papers.conclusion: Cross-modal processing in multilingual speech-text models is both time-dependent and function-dependent, highlighting the importance of generation-aware diagnostics for evaluating multilingual behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal language alignment for language-representation neurons is strongest at the first decoding step but weakens as generation proceeds, indicating a shift from shared to modality-specific processing.
Language-control neurons identified from speech transfer causally to text generation, revealing partially shared circuitry for output-language control.
The cross-modal effect ratio for language control increases at later decoding steps, showing stronger transfer of control mechanisms.
The distribution of language-selective neurons shifts from self-attention to cross-attention as decoding proceeds, indicating a transition from encoder-driven to autoregressive processing.
Cross-modal neuron overlap shows a strong diagonal (same-language) preference at the first step, which weakens at later steps.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model architecture (SeamlessM4T v2).
Reliance on AP-based neuron identification, which captures statistical associations but does not establish causal necessity.
Use of synthetic speech to control for acoustic variability, which may not fully reflect natural speech.
Asymmetries across tasks (e.g., ASR vs. text repetition) and language tags might introduce noise in neuron identification and cross-modal comparisons.
future_direction: Verify whether similar patterns hold for natural speech.
Explore more symmetric settings, such as En→X translation across modalities.
papers.abstract: Multilingual speech-text foundation models aim to process language uniformly across both modality and language, yet it remains unclear whether they internally represent the same language consistently when it is spoken versus written. We investigate this question in SeamlessM4T v2 through three complementary analyses that probe where language and modality information is encoded, how selective neurons causally influence decoding, and how concentrated this influence is across the network. We identify language- and modality-selective neurons using average-precision ranking, investigate their functional role via median-replacement interventions at inference time, and analyze activation-magnitude inequality across languages and modalities. Across experiments, we find evidence of incomplete modality invariance. Although encoder representations become increasingly language-agnostic, this compression makes it more difficult for the shared decoder to recover the language of origin when constructing modality-agnostic representations, particularly when adapting from speech to text. We further observe sharply localized modality-selective structure in cross-attention key and value projections. Finally, speech-conditioned decoding and non-dominant scripts exhibit higher activation concentration, indicating heavier reliance on a small subset of neurons, which may underlie increased brittleness across modalities and languages.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Using Neural Networks to Generate Inferential Roles for Natural Language
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be used to generate inferential roles for natural language, i.e., predict which sentences are likely to follow from a given sentence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a tree-structured neural network can be trained to generate inferential roles (entailments) for sentences, and argues for an inferentialist approach to semantics where meaning is characterized by inferential relations.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can be used to formalize an inferentialist approach to semantics, where the meaning of a linguistic expression is characterized by the inferential roles it plays.
papers.key_findings:
The model generates plausible entailments for novel sentences, as indicated by human plausibility ratings.
Human ratings show model-generated entailments are rated positively and closer to human-generated entailments than contradictions.
The model can generate chains of entailments, building inferential networks around a sentence.
The model can interpolate between known examples to produce novel inferential transitions.
The model can be conditioned on queries to generate specific entailments, demonstrating selective navigation of inferential roles.
papers.limitation:
Generated sentences are sometimes defective (e.g., agreement errors, misplaced words) or incomprehensible.
The model does not consider the relationship between linguistic expressions and the non-linguistic world.
future_direction: Using increased amounts of training data.
Using more sophisticated network architectures (e.g., Tree LSTM, Recursive Neural Tensor Network, lifted matrix-space model).
Incorporating non-linguistic perceptions and actions to account for the relationship between language and the world.
papers.abstract: Neural networks have long been used to study linguistic phenomena spanning the domains of phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics. Of these domains, semantics is somewhat unique in that there is little clarity concerning what a model needs to be able to do in order to provide an account of how the meanings of complex linguistic expressions, such as sentences, are understood. We argue that one thing such models need to be able to do is generate predictions about which further sentences are likely to follow from a given sentence; these define the sentence's "inferential role." We then show that it is possible to train a tree-structured neural network model to generate very simple examples of such inferential roles using the recently released Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) dataset. On an empirical front, we evaluate the performance of this model by reporting entailment prediction accuracies on a set of test sentences not present in the training data. We also report the results of a simple study that compares human plausibility ratings for both human-generated and model-generated entailments for a random selection of sentences in this test set. On a more theoretical front, we argue in favor of a revision to some common assumptions about semantics: understanding a linguistic expression is not only a matter of mapping it onto a representation that somehow constitutes its meaning; rather, understanding a linguistic expression is mainly a matter of being able to draw certain inferences. Inference should accordingly be at the core of any model of semantic cognition.

papers.title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention change when fine-tuned? The paper investigates this through a proposed analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for testing hypotheses about how transformer models encode linguistic phenomena, using unsupervised probes, downstream control tasks, and cross-dataset consistency. Applying it to negation scope reveals evidence of the hypothesized encoding in base models but not in large models.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a procedure and analysis methods to test hypotheses about how transformer-based models encode linguistic phenomena. Applying this to negation scope finds evidence of an interpretable encoding (in-scope words attend to the negation cue) in BERT-base and RoBERTa-base, but weaker evidence in the large models.
papers.key_findings:
Before fine-tuning, several attention heads are sensitive to negation scope, with the best BERT-base head achieving an F1 of 53.8 in a fully unsupervised setting.
There is consistency in which heads are negation-sensitive across different datasets.
After fine-tuning on a negation scope task, the average sensitivity of attention heads improved over the pretrained model for all four models, but only the two base models improved more than a control task.
Attention heads that had the top F1s in the pretrained model do not have the top-ranked improvements after fine-tuning on negation scope.
The behavior of individual attention heads becomes more consistent across datasets after fine-tuning on the negation task, compared to the pretrained model and the control task, except for RoBERTa-large.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses on one interpretable way of encoding negation scope knowledge, but there could be many other ways.
The study uses a single nonlinguistic control task, but one could imagine exploring a gradient of fine-tuning tasks.
The analysis focuses primarily on the attention mechanism, but does not explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to.
future_direction: Explore other hypothesized encodings of negation scope, such as a tree of attention leading to the negation cue.
Explore attention head changes with a gradient of fine-tuning tasks that are more or less relevant to the linguistic phenomenon.
Explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to, since these form the outputs and are more directly tied to classification decisions.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models like BERT, after fine-tuning to a downstream task, have achieved high performance on a variety of NLP problems. Yet explaining their decisions is difficult despite recent work probing their internal representations. We propose a procedure and analysis methods that take a hypothesis of how a transformer-based model might encode a linguistic phenomenon, and test the validity of that hypothesis based on a comparison between knowledge-related downstream tasks with downstream control tasks, and measurement of cross-dataset consistency. We apply this methodology to test BERT and RoBERTa on a hypothesis that some attention heads will consistently attend from a word in negation scope to the negation cue. We find that after fine-tuning BERT and RoBERTa on a negation scope task, the average attention head improves its sensitivity to negation and its attention consistency across negation datasets compared to the pre-trained models. However, only the base models (not the large models) improve compared to a control task, indicating there is evidence for a shallow encoding of negation only in the base models.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Converging to a Lingua Franca: Evolution of Linguistic Regions and Semantics Alignment in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally achieve cross-lingual skill transfer through neuron activation patterns and semantic alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual LLMs develop a common semantic latent space ('Lingua Franca') for processing inputs across languages, with alignment improving through training and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide insights into the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling, offering a foundation for improving cross-lingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron activation patterns are similar for inputs in the same language, revealing key linguistic regions that can be identified and deactivated to impair language-specific performance.
Activation patterns are similar for semantically identical sentences in different languages, indicating mapping to a common semantic space ('Lingua Franca').
With training, key linguistic regions become smaller and activation patterns become more language-agnostic.
Semantic alignment strengthens with training and increased model size, enhancing cross-lingual reasoning ability.
Key neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on BLOOM and LLaMA2 models, may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on specific datasets like Bible and XL-Sum, which may not cover all linguistic nuances.
Methodology based on averaged activation patterns and z-scores may not capture all neuron interactions.
Underlying reasons for patterns remain speculative, requiring further research for causal relationships.
future_direction: Examine a broader range of multilingual LLM architectures.
Utilize more diverse datasets, including low-resource languages.
Apply more sophisticated techniques like causal inference methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, particularly in multilingual contexts. While recent studies suggest that LLMs can transfer skills learned in one language to others, the internal mechanisms behind this ability remain unclear. We observed that the neuron activation patterns of LLMs exhibit similarities when processing the same language, revealing the existence and location of key linguistic regions. Additionally, we found that neuron activation patterns are similar when processing sentences with the same semantic meaning in different languages. This indicates that LLMs map semantically identical inputs from different languages into a "Lingua Franca", a common semantic latent space that allows for consistent processing across languages. This semantic alignment becomes more pronounced with training and increased model size, resulting in a more language-agnostic activation pattern. Moreover, we found that key linguistic neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers of LLMs, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses. Experiments on BLOOM and LLaMA2 support these findings, highlighting the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling up. This paper provides insights into the internal workings of LLMs, offering a foundation for future improvements in their cross-lingual capabilities.

papers.title: A Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability (MI) for transformer-based language models, organizing the field from a task-centric perspective and presenting a beginner's roadmap to guide newcomers.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes the current state of mechanistic interpretability for transformer-based LMs, highlights existing challenges, and outlines promising future research directions to advance the field.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability research can be organized around three fundamental objects of study: features, circuits, and universality.
The field has developed a variety of techniques, including vocabulary projection, intervention-based methods, and sparse autoencoders, each with distinct advantages and limitations.
MI has yielded insights into model capabilities such as in-context learning, reasoning, and knowledge mechanisms, and has applications in model enhancement and AI safety.
Current challenges include the scalability of techniques, the need for standardized benchmarks, and the practical utility of MI findings.
Future directions include advancing MI techniques, improving automated hypothesis generation, and exploring new paradigms of human-AI collaboration.
future_direction: Advancement in MI techniques to improve scalability and generalizability.
Development of standardized benchmarks and metrics for evaluating interpretability methods.
Exploration of automated hypothesis generation and new paradigms of human-AI collaboration driven by MI.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is an emerging sub-field of interpretability that seeks to understand a neural network model by reverse-engineering its internal computations. Recently, MI has garnered significant attention for interpreting transformer-based language models (LMs), resulting in many novel insights yet introducing new challenges. However, there has not been work that comprehensively reviews these insights and challenges, particularly as a guide for newcomers to this field. To fill this gap, we provide a comprehensive survey from a task-centric perspective, organizing the taxonomy of MI research around specific research questions or tasks. We outline the fundamental objects of study in MI, along with the techniques, evaluation methods, and key findings for each task in the taxonomy. In particular, we present a task-centric taxonomy as a roadmap for beginners to navigate the field by helping them quickly identify impactful problems in which they are most interested and leverage MI for their benefit. Finally, we discuss the current gaps in the field and suggest potential future directions for MI research.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Sharing Matters: Analysing Neurons Across Languages and Tasks in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is neuron activation shared across tasks and languages in multilingual large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a fine-grained neuron classification method for multilingual LLMs and demonstrates that neurons shared across all languages (all-shared neurons) are crucial for model performance and generating accurate responses.
papers.conclusion: The study improves understanding of the internal workings of multilingual LLMs by showing the pivotal role of cross-lingually shared neurons and the task- and model-dependent nature of neuron activation patterns, paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating all-shared neurons significantly decreases model performance across tasks (up to 87.39% drop in accuracy).
All-shared neurons have the greatest impact on generating both answers and correct answers, as measured by Generation Impact Score and Correctness Impact Score.
Neuron activation patterns vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages; for example, instruction-finetuned models show more all-shared neurons than foundation models.
Neuron sharing does not always align with language similarity; languages from the same family do not necessarily share more neurons.
Deactivating certain neuron types (partial-shared or specific) can occasionally improve performance for some languages, possibly due to mitigating knowledge conflicts.
future_direction: More in-depth investigation of how factual knowledge is stored and shared across languages in LLMs.
Further exploration of the relationship between language similarity and neuron sharing.
Investigation of whether in-context learning leads to better neuron activation composition rather than invoking more neurons.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), and recent studies have aimed to understand their underlying mechanisms. However, most of this research is conducted within a monolingual setting, primarily focusing on English. Few studies have attempted to explore the internal workings of LLMs in multilingual settings. In this study, we aim to fill this research gap by examining how neuron activation is shared across tasks and languages. We classify neurons into four distinct categories based on their responses to a specific input across different languages: all-shared, partial-shared, specific, and non-activated. Building upon this categorisation, we conduct extensive experiments on three tasks across nine languages using several LLMs and present an in-depth analysis in this work. Our findings reveal that: (i) deactivating the all-shared neurons significantly decreases performance; (ii) the shared neurons play a vital role in generating responses, especially for the all-shared neurons; (iii) neuron activation patterns are highly sensitive and vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages. These findings shed light on the internal workings of multilingual LLMs and pave the way for future research. We release the code to foster research in this area.

papers.title: Beyond Components: Singular Vector-Based Interpretability of Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: Can transformer components (attention heads and MLPs) be decomposed into orthogonal singular directions that reveal superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a directional interpretability perspective that decomposes transformer components into orthogonal singular directions, showing that multiple low-rank, interpretable computations coexist within single attention heads and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed, opening new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of learned singular directions can faithfully preserve model behavior.
These directions align with meaningful subfunctions, e.g., in IOI, name mover heads encode multiple overlapping subfunctions along distinct singular directions.
Components identified as part of known circuits exhibit strong engagement along specific singular directions, indicating computations are embedded in compact subspaces.
Transformer computations are distributed, structured, and compositional, with overlapping subfunctions embedded within shared subspaces.
Singular directions can be used for controlled interventions, e.g., in gender pronoun resolution, scaling directions can modify predictions.
papers.limitation: Some directions remain challenging to interpret fully.
future_direction: Conduct targeted intervention experiments to validate causal contributions of discovered components.
Examine whether these mechanisms generalize to larger or more capable models (e.g., Phi, LLaMA).
Explore activation of these mechanisms in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit complex and distributed behavior, yet their internal computations remain poorly understood. Existing mechanistic interpretability methods typically treat attention heads and multilayer perceptron layers (MLPs) (the building blocks of a transformer architecture) as indivisible units, overlooking possibilities of functional substructure learned within them. In this work, we introduce a more fine-grained perspective that decomposes these components into orthogonal singular directions, revealing superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP. We validate our perspective on widely used standard tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI), Gender Pronoun (GP), and Greater Than (GT), showing that previously identified canonical functional heads, such as the name mover, encode multiple overlapping subfunctions aligned with distinct singular directions. Nodes in a computational graph, that are previously identified as circuit elements show strong activation along specific low-rank directions, suggesting that meaningful computations reside in compact subspaces. While some directions remain challenging to interpret fully, our results highlight that transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed. This perspective opens new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability and a deeper understanding of model internals.

papers.title: Function Induction and Task Generalization: An Interpretability Study with Off-by-One Addition
papers.research_question: What mechanisms inside large language models drive task-level generalization via in-context learning, specifically through the lens of off-by-one addition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'function induction' mechanism in transformer language models that explains how they generalize from seen to unseen tasks via in-context learning, particularly for multi-step tasks like off-by-one addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition is explained by a circuit resembling induction heads but operating at a function level, termed 'function induction'.
The induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads (FI heads) in parallel, each emitting a distinct piece of the function.
The same function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including shifted multiple-choice QA, Caesar cipher, and base-8 addition.
The circuit involves three groups of attention heads: consolidation heads (Group 1), function induction heads (Group 2), and previous token heads (Group 3).
The mechanism is found across multiple models (Gemma-2, Mistral, Llama-2, Llama-3), though with variations.
papers.limitation: The exact role of consolidation heads and why they emerge remains limited, relating to the broader challenge of interpreting 'negative' behavior in language models.
future_direction: Finer-grained interpretation of consolidation heads and their role.
Further investigation into the differences between FI heads and FV heads (function vector heads).
Training toy models to perform off-by-one addition and isolating the circuit requires separate study.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate the intriguing ability to perform unseen tasks via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear what mechanisms inside the model drive such task-level generalization. In this work, we approach this question through the lens of off-by-one addition (i.e., 1+1=3, 2+2=5, 3+3=?), a two-step, counterfactual task with an unexpected +1 function as a second step. Leveraging circuit-style interpretability techniques such as path patching, we analyze the models' internal computations behind their performance and present three key findings. First, we uncover a function induction mechanism that explains the model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition. This mechanism resembles the structure of the induction head mechanism found in prior work and elevates it to a higher level of abstraction. Second, we show that the induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads in parallel, each of which emits a distinct piece of the +1 function. Finally, we find that this function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including synthetic tasks such as shifted multiple-choice QA and algorithmic tasks such as base-8 addition. Overall, our findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Contextualize-then-Aggregate: Circuits for In-Context Learning in Gemma-2 2B
papers.research_question: What mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a few-shot prompt during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a two-step 'contextualize-then-aggregate' circuit for in-context learning in Gemma-2, where lower layers contextualize individual few-shot examples and higher layers aggregate this information to predict the next token.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a two-stage procedure for in-context learning where the model contextualizes representations of individual few-shot examples before aggregating them to prepare the next-token prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The model uses a two-step strategy: contextualization of individual few-shot examples in lower layers, followed by aggregation of task information in higher layers.
The aggregation step alone is insufficient for full performance on some tasks; contextualization is crucial, especially with ambiguous examples.
The identified circuits recover at least 90% of the full model's performance across five ICL tasks.
The information transported differs by edge type: aggregation edges generally move task information, while contextualization edges move information about input/output spaces.
The importance and specific edges of the contextualization subcircuit vary between tasks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to five tasks and one model family (Gemma-2).
Circuit discovery relies on patching, which requires careful design of counterfactual inputs.
The study does not provide a full interpretation of all individual components in the model.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more tasks and models.
Investigate the role of contextualization in other settings, such as linear regression tasks.
Provide a more fine-grained interpretation of individual components.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) is an intriguing ability of large language models (LLMs). Despite a substantial amount of work on its behavioral aspects and how it emerges in miniature setups, it remains unclear which mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a fewshot prompt. We use causal interventions to identify information flow in Gemma-2 2B for five naturalistic ICL tasks. We find that the model infers task information using a two-step strategy we call contextualize-then-aggregate: In the lower layers, the model builds up representations of individual fewshot examples, which are contextualized by preceding examples through connections between fewshot input and output tokens across the sequence. In the higher layers, these representations are aggregated to identify the task and prepare prediction of the next output. The importance of the contextualization step differs between tasks, and it may become more important in the presence of ambiguous examples. Overall, by providing rigorous causal analysis, our results shed light on the mechanisms through which ICL happens in language models.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models with applications to the financial services industry
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to understand the inner workings of large language models for financial services applications, specifically for compliance monitoring?
papers.core_contribution: This paper pioneers the application of mechanistic interpretability to financial services, designing algorithmic tasks for compliance monitoring and analyzing GPT-2 Small's attention patterns for identifying potential Fair Lending violations.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability techniques can be successfully applied to understand LLM behavior in financial compliance tasks, providing insights into the roles of specific attention heads and MLP layers.
papers.key_findings:
Heads 11.4, 8.9, and 6.3 contribute positively to the Fair Lending task completion, while heads 0.6, 11.0, and 10.7 contribute negatively.
MLP layers 2 and 4 significantly improve task completion, while MLP layer 10 and attention layer 0 decrease performance.
Activation patching reveals that heads 10.2, 10.7, and 11.3 (positive) and heads 9.6 and 10.6 (negative) play significant roles, with head 10.2's value vector being particularly important.
The Fair Lending compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, involving information processing across many layers rather than being localized to a few final layers.
Value patching has a more significant effect than key or query patching for important heads in later layers (9-11).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to GPT-2 Small, a relatively small model, and may not generalize to larger, more powerful LLMs.
The financial compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, making circuit discovery more challenging and less localized.
future_direction: Conducting experiments with more powerful open-source LLMs such as Mistral 7B and Llama-2 7B.
Working on more algorithmic examples of compliance tasks in financial services and finding prompts that result in large logit differences.
Performing path patching as a more sophisticated circuit discovery approach for end-to-end circuit identification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit remarkable capabilities across a broad spectrum of applications. Nevertheless, due to their intrinsic complexity, these models present substantial challenges in interpreting their internal decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses critical challenges when it comes to their adaptation by financial institutions, where concerns and accountability regarding bias, fairness, and reliability are of paramount importance. Mechanistic interpretability aims at reverse engineering complex AI models such as transformers. In this paper, we are pioneering the use of mechanistic interpretability to shed some light on the inner workings of large language models for use in financial services applications. We offer several examples of how algorithmic tasks can be designed for compliance monitoring purposes. In particular, we investigate GPT-2 Small’s attention pattern when prompted to identify potential violation of Fair Lending laws. Using direct logit attribution, we study the contributions of each layer and its corresponding attention heads to the logit difference in the residual stream. Finally, we design clean and corrupted prompts and use activation patching as a causal intervention method to localize our task completion components further. We observe that the (positive) heads 10.2 (head 2, layer 10), 10.7, and 11.3, as well as the (negative) heads 9.6 and 10.6 play a significant role in the task completion.

papers.title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)'s "Interpretability Illusion" Arguments
papers.research_question: Are the phenomena identified by Makelov et al. (2023) as 'interpretability illusions' actually inherent properties of distributed representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the 'interpretability illusions' identified by Makelov et al. (2023) are not illusions but inherent properties of distributed representations, and provides additional experiments using DAS to analyze causal mechanisms in GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The phenomena labeled as 'interpretability illusions' are inherent to distributed representations, and the work by Makelov et al. (2023) has advanced the field of mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Even directions considered non-illusory by Makelov et al. can be classified as illusory under their own definition.
The illusions reported by Makelov et al. are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms.
DAS can reproduce and extend findings on the IOI task, showing that name position information in GPT-2 is distributed across attention heads and emerges in the 8th layer.
Name position information is not carried by MLP activations but by the self-attention block in the 8th layer.
The correct IO name representation is distributed across multiple attention heads in the 9th layer.
papers.abstract: We respond to the recent paper by Makelov et al.
