(2023), which reviews subspace interchange intervention methods like distributed alignment search (DAS; Geiger et al. 2023) and claims that these methods potentially cause "interpretability illusions". We first review Makelov et al. (2023)'s technical notion of what an "interpretability illusion" is, and then we show that even intuitive and desirable explanations can qualify as illusions in this sense. As a result, their method of discovering "illusions" can reject explanations they consider "non-illusory". We then argue that the illusions Makelov et al. (2023) see in practice are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms. We close by emphasizing that, though we disagree with their core characterization, Makelov et al. (2023)'s examples and discussion have undoubtedly pushed the field of interpretability forward.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Findings of the BlackboxNLP 2025 Shared Task: Localizing Circuits and Causal Variables in Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper reports the results of the BlackboxNLP 2025 Shared Task, which used the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (MIB) to evaluate methods for circuit localization and causal variable localization in language models. It finds that ensembling and regularization strategies improve circuit discovery, and non-linear projections improve causal variable localization.
papers.conclusion: The shared task demonstrated that ensembling and regularization are promising directions for circuit discovery, and non-linear projections can improve causal variable localization, though more controls are needed to ensure learned features capture genuine model variables. The MIB leaderboard will continue to accept submissions to facilitate progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Ensembling strategies (parallel, sequential, hybrid) and regularization techniques (filtering unstable components) proved effective for circuit localization, achieving strong CPR and CMD scores.
Non-linear featurizers (using MLPs and activation functions) and orthogonal non-linear projections significantly improved causal variable localization over baseline methods like DAS.
The best method for circuit localization depended on the chosen metric (CPR vs. CMD), with no single method dominating across all tasks and models.
The shared task received a relatively small number of submissions, indicating room for broader community participation and method development.
The MIB leaderboard remains open for ongoing submissions, providing a standardized framework for future mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The shared task received a relatively small number of submissions, which may limit the generalizability of the findings.
For causal variable localization, non-linear featurizers are highly expressive and could learn features not actually present in the model, requiring additional validation to ensure they capture genuine causal variables.
future_direction: Continue exploring ensembling strategies and regularization techniques for circuit discovery.
Develop more expressive featurizer training formulations that leverage existing mediator types for causal variable localization, while ensuring proper controls to isolate concepts truly in the model.
Conduct detailed comparisons of methods on more fine-grained distributions to characterize when and why each method is likely to succeed, and compare compute requirements.
papers.abstract: Dana Arad, Yonatan Belinkov, Hanjie Chen, Najoung Kim, Hosein Mohebbi, Aaron Mueller, Gabriele Sarti, Martin Tutek. Proceedings of the 8th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP. 2025.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Investigating The Functional Roles of Attention Heads in Vision Language Models: Evidence for Reasoning Modules
papers.research_question: What functional roles do attention heads in vision-language models play in multimodal reasoning, and how are they organized?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing-based interpretability framework and the CogVision dataset to identify functional attention heads in VLMs, revealing that these heads are sparse, universal, and causally important for multimodal reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that their framework provides insights into the functional organization of attention mechanisms in VLMs and suggests directions for more interpretable and cognitively inspired models.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in VLMs can be associated with specific cognitive functions (e.g., math reasoning, visual reception) through probing.
Functional heads are sparse (only a small subset of heads are highly important for each function).
These functional heads are universal across different VLM architectures and scales.
Functional heads exhibit cross-function interactions and hierarchical organization.
Intervention experiments (masking, activation patching) show that functional heads are causally important for reasoning performance.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on eight predefined cognitive functions, which may not cover the full spectrum of LLM capabilities.
The analysis concentrates on attention heads, leaving other components such as MLPs unexplored.
future_direction: Expand the taxonomy of cognitive functions to include finer-grained or emergent functions.
Extend the analysis to other model components such as MLPs.
Further explore advanced probing methods.
papers.abstract: Despite excelling on multimodal benchmarks, vision-language models (VLMs) largely remain a black box. In this paper, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the internal mechanisms of VLMs, focusing on the functional roles of attention heads in multimodal reasoning. To this end, we introduce CogVision, a dataset that decomposes complex multimodal questions into step-by-step subquestions designed to simulate human reasoning through a chain-of-thought paradigm, with each subquestion associated with specific receptive or cognitive functions such as high-level visual reception and inference. Using a probing-based methodology, we identify attention heads that specialize in these functions and characterize them as functional heads. Our analysis across diverse VLM families reveals that these functional heads are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across functions, and mediate interactions and hierarchical organization. Furthermore, intervention experiments demonstrate their critical role in multimodal reasoning: removing functional heads leads to performance degradation, while emphasizing them enhances accuracy. These findings provide new insights into the cognitive organization of VLMs and suggest promising directions for designing models with more human-aligned perceptual and reasoning abilities.

papers.title: Models of Visually Grounded Speech Signal Pay Attention to Nouns: A Bilingual Experiment on English and Japanese
papers.research_question: What is the behavior of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on English and Japanese, and does it focus on nouns?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that attention in neural models of visually grounded speech focuses on nouns across English and Japanese, and demonstrates cross-lingual speech retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that attention in visually grounded speech models focuses on nouns across languages, with language-specific adaptations, and enables cross-lingual retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.key_findings:
Attention primarily focuses on nouns in both English and Japanese models.
The Japanese model also pays attention to particles, developing a language-specific behavior similar to human toddlers.
Attention peaks are located at word endings in English and at both beginnings and endings in Japanese.
Images can be used as pivots for cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval without parallel data.
The model exhibits noun-bias, aligning with theories of child language acquisition.
papers.limitation: The study uses synthetic speech with only one voice, whereas prior work used real speech with multiple speakers.
future_direction: Validate the methodology on a bilingual dataset featuring real voices.
Extract a bilingual speech-to-speech dictionary using attention peaks as anchor points.
papers.abstract: We investigate the behaviour of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on two languages: English and Japanese. Experimental results show that attention focuses on nouns and this behaviour holds true for two very typologically different languages. We also draw parallels between artificial neural attention and human attention and show that neural attention focuses on word endings as it has been theorised for human attention. Finally, we investigate how two visually grounded monolingual models can be used to perform cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval. For both languages, the enriched bilingual (speech-image) corpora with part-of-speech tags and forced alignments are distributed to the community for reproducible research.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: Sensitivity Meets Sparsity: The Impact of Extremely Sparse Parameter Patterns on Theory-of-Mind of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which parameters in LLMs are sensitive to Theory-of-Mind capabilities, and how do these parameters influence ToM reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameters in LLMs and shows that perturbing them degrades ToM performance, contextual localization, and language understanding by disrupting dominant-frequency activations in RoPE-based positional encoding.
papers.conclusion: The insights provide a deeper understanding of how LLMs acquire social reasoning abilities, bridging AI interpretability with cognitive science, with implications for enhancing model alignment, mitigating biases, and improving AI systems for human interaction.
papers.key_findings:
An extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameter pattern exists, and perturbing it significantly affects ToM capabilities, contextual localization, and language understanding.
The functionality of the ToM-sensitive parameter pattern is linked to the positional encoding module (RoPE), and perturbing it disrupts dominant-frequency activations.
Perturbing the ToM-sensitive parameter pattern affects the attention mechanism by altering the angle between q and kBOS, shifting attention sinks, and impairing language understanding.
papers.limitation: The method is only effective for RoPE-based models and does not generalize to non-RoPE models.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the emergence of Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities in large language models (LLMs) from a mechanistic perspective, focusing on the role of extremely sparse parameter patterns. We introduce a novel method to identify ToM-sensitive parameters and reveal that perturbing as little as 0.001% of these parameters significantly degrades ToM performance while also impairing contextual localization and language understanding. To understand this effect, we analyze their interaction with core architectural components of LLMs. Our findings demonstrate that these sensitive parameters are closely linked to the positional encoding module, particularly in models using Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), where perturbations disrupt dominant-frequency activations critical for contextual processing. Furthermore, we show that perturbing ToM-sensitive parameters affects LLM's attention mechanism by modulating the angle between queries and keys under positional encoding. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how LLMs acquire social reasoning abilities, bridging AI interpretability with cognitive science. Our results have implications for enhancing model alignment, mitigating biases, and improving AI systems designed for human interaction.

papers.title: Language over Content: Tracing Cultural Understanding in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally represent and process cultural knowledge, and does linguistic form or semantic content dominate their internal path selection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that internal activation paths in multilingual LLMs overlap more for semantically equivalent questions asked in the same language about different cultures than for questions asked in different languages about the same culture, indicating that cultural understanding is strongly mediated by language-specific circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query language affects internal path selection more strongly than target culture, and cultural understanding is mainly stored in language-dependent paths. Politically unique contexts like South and North Korea are reflected in the model's internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Internal path overlap is greater for same-language, cross-country questions than for cross-language, same-country questions, showing a strong language-specific pattern.
The South Korea–North Korea pair exhibits low path overlap and high variability despite linguistic similarity, indicating distinct internal representation patterns.
Multilingual LLMs rely heavily on language-specific circuits when representing and applying cultural knowledge, prioritizing linguistic form over semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on internal path overlap, but interventions or circuit patching could clarify which features drive cultural knowledge processing and how language- and culture-related features interact.
Some country pairs, such as South and North Koreas, show distinct patterns compared to other similar language pairs, yet the reasons remain unclear.
future_direction: Further subdivide cultural knowledge into finer categories and include more languages for a more comprehensive investigation.
Use interventions or circuit patching to clarify which features drive cultural knowledge processing and how language- and culture-related features interact.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used across diverse cultural contexts, making accurate cultural understanding essential. Prior evaluations have mostly focused on output-level performance, obscuring the factors that drive differences in responses, while studies using circuit analysis have covered few languages and rarely focused on culture. In this work, we trace LLMs' internal cultural understanding mechanisms by measuring activation path overlaps when answering semantically equivalent questions under two conditions: varying the target country while fixing the question language, and varying the question language while fixing the country. We also use same-language country pairs to disentangle language from cultural aspects. Results show that internal paths overlap more for same-language, cross-country questions than for cross-language, same-country questions, indicating strong language-specific patterns. Notably, the South Korea-North Korea pair exhibits low overlap and high variability, showing that linguistic similarity does not guarantee aligned internal representation.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: InverseScope: Scalable Activation Inversion for Interpreting Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to interpret neural activations in large language models via input inversion with minimal assumptions, and scale this approach to larger models and practical tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InverseScope, a scalable activation inversion framework for interpreting LLMs with minimal assumptions, enabling systematic and quantitative analysis of internal representations.
papers.conclusion: InverseScope scales inversion-based interpretability to larger LLMs, providing a rigorous framework for analyzing feature representations and offering new mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
InverseScope significantly improves sampling efficiency over prior inversion methods, reducing refusal rates.
In the IOI task, it identifies attention heads that encode object and subject features, aligning with known circuits.
It outperforms sparse autoencoders in attribute identification on the RAVEL dataset.
In ICL tasks, it explains the emergence of task vectors by showing the separation of task and query features in attention layers.
papers.limitation:
Does not scale to long input sequences.
Hypothesis generation still requires human involvement.
future_direction: Scaling to long input sequences
Automating hypothesis generation
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) is a central challenge in interpretability research. Existing feature interpretability methods often rely on strong assumptions about the structure of representations that may not hold in practice. In this work, we introduce InverseScope, an assumption-light and scalable framework for interpreting neural activations via input inversion. Given a target activation, we define a distribution over inputs that generate similar activations and analyze this distribution to infer the encoded information. To address the inefficiency of sampling in high-dimensional spaces, we propose a novel conditional generation architecture that significantly improves sample efficiency compared to previous method. We further introduce a quantitative evaluation protocol that tests interpretability hypotheses using the feature consistency rate computed over the sampled inputs. InverseScope scales inversion-based interpretability methods to larger models and practical tasks, enabling systematic and quantitative analysis of internal representations in real-world LLMs.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Mitigation of Language Confusion in English-Centric Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does language confusion arise mechanistically in English-centric LLMs, and can it be mitigated through neuron-level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first mechanistic interpretability study of language confusion in LLMs, revealing that confusion points arise from transition failures in final layers and can be effectively mitigated by editing a small set of critical neurons identified through comparative analysis.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first mechanistic interpretability account of language confusion in English-centric LLMs, demonstrating that targeted neuron editing can robustly mitigate confusion without sacrificing general competence or fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Confusion points are critical drivers of language confusion, and token replacement at these points reduces confusion.
Layer-wise analysis shows that language confusion is caused by failed transitions to the target language in the final layers.
Neuron-level analysis identifies specific FFN neurons in late layers that are responsible for confusion points.
Comparative importance selection of neurons enables effective mitigation of language confusion through editing.
Neuron editing achieves confusion reduction comparable to multilingual tuning for many languages while preserving general competence and output quality.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on the monolingual setting; cross-lingual contexts are left for future research.
Neuron editing interventions may require further validation across broader domains and model architectures.
Fully understanding how these mechanisms interact with other multilingual phenomena warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Extending analysis to cross-lingual contexts
Validating neuron editing across broader domains and model architectures
Investigating interactions with other multilingual phenomena
papers.abstract: Language confusion -- where large language models (LLMs) generate unintended languages against the user's need -- remains a critical challenge, especially for English-centric models. We present the first mechanistic interpretability (MI) study of language confusion, combining behavioral benchmarking with neuron-level analysis. Using the Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB), we show that confusion points (CPs) -- specific positions where language switches occur -- are central to this phenomenon. Through layer-wise analysis with TunedLens and targeted neuron attribution, we reveal that transition failures in the final layers drive confusion. We further demonstrate that editing a small set of critical neurons, identified via comparative analysis with a multilingual-tuned counterpart, substantially mitigates confusion while largely preserving general competence and fluency. Our approach matches multilingual alignment in confusion reduction for many languages and yields cleaner, higher-quality outputs. These findings provide new insights into the internal dynamics of LLMs and highlight neuron-level interventions as a promising direction for robust, interpretable multilingual language modeling. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ercong21/lang_confusion.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs struggle to detect arithmetic errors in their own outputs, and what internal mechanisms are responsible for error detection?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs have a structural dissociation between arithmetic computation (in higher layers) and validation (in middle layers), relying on consistency heads for surface-level alignment checks, which explains their difficulty in error detection.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability provides valuable insights into how LLMs detect or fail to detect arithmetic errors, and the validation gap arises from structural dissociation between computation and validation.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for arithmetic error detection are structurally similar across different models.
Error detection is governed by consistency heads—attention heads in lower to middle layers that check surface-level alignment of numerical values.
Arithmetic computation occurs in higher layers, while validation takes place in middle layers, leading to a structural dissociation.
Patching a small subset of consistency heads can control the model's error detection behavior.
Adding latent activations from higher layers to the residual stream in lower layers significantly enhances error detection, closing the validation gap.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to smaller LLMs and basic math word problems.
Circuit discovery may not be complete, i.e., identified circuits might not include all components involved in the task behavior.
future_direction: Study error detection in larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: The ability of large language models (LLMs) to validate their output and identify potential errors is crucial for ensuring robustness and reliability. However, current research indicates that LLMs struggle with self-correction, encountering significant challenges in detecting errors. While studies have explored methods to enhance self-correction in LLMs, relatively little attention has been given to understanding the models' internal mechanisms underlying error detection. In this paper, we present a mechanistic analysis of error detection in LLMs, focusing on simple arithmetic problems. Through circuit analysis, we identify the computational subgraphs responsible for detecting arithmetic errors across four smaller-sized LLMs. Our findings reveal that all models heavily rely on $\textit{consistency heads}$--attention heads that assess surface-level alignment of numerical values in arithmetic solutions. Moreover, we observe that the models' internal arithmetic computation primarily occurs in higher layers, whereas validation takes place in middle layers, before the final arithmetic results are fully encoded. This structural dissociation between arithmetic computation and validation seems to explain why smaller-sized LLMs struggle to detect even simple arithmetic errors.

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Evaluating Contrast Localizer for Identifying Causal Units in Social & Mathematical Tasks in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the contrast localizer method reliably identify causally relevant units for Theory of Mind and mathematical reasoning tasks in LLMs and VLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that contrast localizers may not reliably identify causally relevant units for specific tasks, as ablation of low-activation units can be more harmful and cross-task interference is observed, suggesting the need for improved localizer designs.
papers.conclusion: The contrast localizer approach has limitations in reliably identifying causally relevant units for specific tasks, indicating a need for broader stimulus sets and more granular analysis of intermediate representations.
papers.key_findings:
Lesioning top-activated units identified by contrast localizers does not consistently cause significant performance drops compared to random or low-activation units.
Lesioning bottom (low-activation) units sometimes leads to larger performance drops than top units, especially on the MATH dataset.
Cross-task analysis shows that units identified by the MD (mathematical) localizer when lesioned cause larger performance drops on ToM tasks than units from the ToM localizer.
The contrast localizer method may not reliably distinguish task-specific units for Theory of Mind and mathematical reasoning tasks.
The findings suggest that broader stimulus sets and more granular analysis (e.g., intermediate representations) may be needed for accurate localization.
papers.limitation:
The current contrast localizer for MD tasks is limited to comparing easy versus hard arithmetic operations, which may not capture the full spectrum of mathematical reasoning.
Focusing solely on output activation units may not be sufficient for dissecting complex reasoning tasks that likely rely on intermediate representations.
future_direction: Extending the localizer stimulus sets to include a broader range of tasks and contrasts.
Examining intermediate representations and hidden activations within each transformer block for more granular analysis.
papers.abstract: This work adapts a neuroscientific contrast localizer to pinpoint causally relevant units for Theory of Mind (ToM) and mathematical reasoning tasks in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs). Across 11 LLMs and 5 VLMs ranging in size from 3B to 90B parameters, we localize top-activated units using contrastive stimulus sets and assess their causal role via targeted ablations. We compare the effect of lesioning functionally selected units against low-activation and randomly selected units on downstream accuracy across established ToM and mathematical benchmarks. Contrary to expectations, low-activation units sometimes produced larger performance drops than the highly activated ones, and units derived from the mathematical localizer often impaired ToM performance more than those from the ToM localizer. These findings call into question the causal relevance of contrast-based localizers and highlight the need for broader stimulus sets and more accurately capture task-specific units.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Multi-speaker Attention Alignment for Multimodal Social Interaction
papers.research_question: Why do Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with multi-speaker social interaction tasks, and how can cross-modal attention alignment be improved to address this?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to strengthen cross-modal attention alignment between visual and textual tokens belonging to the same speaker in MLLMs, improving performance on multi-speaker social interaction tasks without adding trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method strengthens cross-modal attention alignment in MLLMs, improving their ability to understand multi-speaker social interactions in videos.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal attention alignment in MLLMs is significantly weaker in multi-speaker videos compared to object-centric images.
The proposed attention alignment method, using dynamic head selection and an adaptive social-aware bias, consistently improves MLLM performance across multiple models and social interaction tasks.
The method successfully focuses model attention on speaker-relevant visual regions, enabling more robust multi-party social reasoning.
Middle transformer layers are most crucial for applying the attention bias, and activating only a subset of heads (10-20%) yields the best performance.
An adaptive bias strength, based on the original attention pattern, performs better than a fixed bias.
papers.limitation:
The method does not surpass state-of-the-art on the speaking target identification task, which may require balancing attention between the current speaker and the speaking target.
The method relies on speaker bounding box annotations, which can be costly to obtain.
future_direction: Further investigate the role of attention heads in cross-modal alignment.
Explore ways to leverage inherent grounding abilities of MLLMs to guide alignment without relying on bounding box annotations.
papers.abstract: Understanding social interaction in video requires reasoning over a dynamic interplay of verbal and non-verbal cues: who is speaking, to whom, and with what gaze or gestures. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are natural candidates, simply adding visual inputs yields surprisingly inconsistent gains on social tasks. Our quantitative analysis of cross-modal attention inside state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals a core failure mode: in multi-speaker scenes, visual and textual tokens lack speaker-consistent alignment, exhibiting substantially weaker cross-modal attention than in object-centric images. To address this, we propose a multimodal multi-speaker attention alignment method that can be integrated into existing MLLMs. First, we introduce dynamic cross-modal head selection to identify attention heads most responsible for grounding. Then, an adaptive social-aware attention bias, computed from existing attention patterns and speaker locations, is injected into the attention mechanism. This bias reinforces alignment between a speaker's visual representation and their utterances without introducing trainable parameters or architectural changes. We integrate our method into three distinct MLLMs (LLaVA-NeXT-Video, Qwen2.5-VL, and InternVL3) and evaluate on three benchmarks (TVQA+, MMSI, OnlineMMSI). Across four social tasks, results demonstrate that our approach improves the ability of MLLMs and achieves state-of-the-art results. Attention visualizations confirm our method successfully focuses the model on speaker-relevant regions, enabling more robust multi-party social reasoning. Our implementation and model will be available at https://github.com/ut-vision/SocialInteraction.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Attention Heads of Large Language Models: A Survey
